title: Cantor Fitzgerald Raises Its CrowdStrike Target to $275. Is It Still Too Low?

 Wiltone Asuncion • 4 minute read Reviewed by: Michael Douglass Last updated Nov 17, 2026 @Corina Ciocirlan's Images via Canva, @sy via Canva
 Key Takeaways
 Cantor Fitzgerald raised its CrowdStrike price target to $275 from $250 on Nov. 16 and kept its Overweight rating. The new target sits about 23% above the stock’s Nov. 16 close.
 The firm points to platform consolidation and faster growth in CrowdStrike’s core endpoint business, after a record quarter for net new ARR.
 At $275, CrowdStrike would trade at about 195x forward earnings. Its five-year average is 111x, and full-year earnings estimates have slipped over the past 90 days.
 Cantor’s target asks for more than today’s estimates support, and the Dec. 1 report is the next test.
 CrowdStrike ( CRWD ) is up 66% in a year, and Wall Street keeps chasing it. Cantor Fitzgerald raised its price target to $275 from $250 on Nov. 16 and kept its Overweight rating, matching the $275 target Rosenblatt set days earlier. That puts Cantor’s target about 23% above the stock’s Nov. 16 close of $223.21.
 A record quarter, then a reset
 In CrowdStrike’s quarter to July 31, net new ARR hit a record $333 million, up 51%. Management raised its full-year net new ARR growth outlook to 34% at the midpoint. The stock went on to a closing high of $278.86 on Oct. 6, then lost 9.9% in one session during a broad tech selloff on Nov. 5. At its Nov. 16 close, it sat 20% below that high.
 Cantor sees the core business speeding up
 Cantor is betting on the business CrowdStrike was built on. The firm cited strong checks, momentum in platform consolidation, accelerating growth in core endpoint detection and response, and continued success in SIEM (security information and event management) and cloud products. That matches the August call, where CEO George Kurtz said “our endpoint business accelerated for the fourth consecutive quarter as customers look to secure their growing AI attack surface.”

 Does $275 add up?
 The 54 analysts covering CrowdStrike have spent the year catching up, and their consensus target nearly doubled, from $128 to $250:
 CrowdStrike (CRWD): analysts’ consensus (mean) price target, $ per share, last year ( TIKR ) 
 Their earnings estimates haven’t kept pace. Analysts expect normalized EPS of $1.26 for the year ending January 2027, right at management’s $1.25 – $1.26 guidance. They expect $1.61 for the year after. Both figures are a couple of cents below where they stood 90 days ago:
 CrowdStrike (CRWD): normalized EPS, actual and consensus estimates, $ per share, fiscal 2024-2028 (years to January) ( TIKR ) 
 Those estimates will likely stay put until CrowdStrike updates its guidance. So the higher targets come down to what investors will pay. CrowdStrike traded at 160x forward earnings at its Nov. 13 close, against a five-year average of 111x:
 CrowdStrike (CRWD): forward (NTM) P/E, last 5 years ( TIKR ) 
 Cantor’s $275 works out to about 195x the $1.41 a share analysts expect over the next twelve months.
 The target already asks a lot
 The biggest risk is the AI labs themselves. When Anthropic launched Claude Code Security on Feb. 20, CrowdStrike fell nearly 8% that day, and OpenAI followed with Codex Security in March.
 So is $275 still too low? Not on today’s numbers. Cantor’s target needs an even higher multiple on estimates that have slipped since the summer.
 That could change on Dec. 1, when CrowdStrike reports after the close. Net new ARR above its $343 – $347 million guidance, plus another full-year raise, would give analysts a reason to lift next year’s numbers. Then $275 would start to look conservative.
